name: Daslang (daScript)
baseline: Lua 5.5.1 (also QuickJS 2026-06-04, LuaJIT with the JIT off, Luau 0.736)
workload: 16 microbenchmark kernels (sha256, dictionary, n-bodies, spectral norm, mandelbrot, exp loop, string2float, particles kinematics, queen, interop host calls, primes loop, tree, sort, fibonacci loop, float2string, fibonacci recursive), each reimplemented per language; median of five processes, each sample runs the kernel as often as fits a 0.5 s budget.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter lane vs Lua 5.5.1 on Linux (Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE): sha256 0.002510 s vs 0.068548 s, n-bodies 0.009163 s vs 0.041577 s, mandelbrot 0.001791 s vs 0.056917 s, tree 0.023617 s vs 0.031137 s, fibonacci recursive 0.048174 s vs 0.048747 s (parity). vs QuickJS on the same board: sha256 0.021312 s, n-bodies 0.082429 s, mandelbrot 0.006346 s. Faster than both Lua and QuickJS on all 16 kernels on both platforms; geometric mean about 4.6x vs Lua and 4.9x vs QuickJS on Linux, 4.7x and 5.4x on Apple M1 Max (derived from page data). The README tables also carry AOT and JIT lanes.
compiler_and_flags: Linux: Clang 19.1.7; macOS: AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101; daslang 0.6.4 on LLVM 22.1.5. The harness CMakeLists forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release when unset and builds Lua 5.5.1 from the official tarball (LUA_USE_LINUX / LUA_USE_MACOSX). I did not verify how the QuickJS, LuaJIT and Luau lanes are built.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE (Linux) and Apple M1 Max (macOS); results captured 2026-09-13
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars (daScript); a Gaijin Entertainment project whose README cites production-game use
tradeoffs: Statically typed language with its own syntax, so Lua or JS scripts cannot be reused. Data layout matches C++, so host calls need no marshaling (interop host calls kernel 0.003740 s vs Lua 0.015360 s). Interpreter startup is slow: hello world 0.026112 s vs Lua 0.002366 s and QuickJS 0.002403 s on Linux (derived from page data). The JIT lane uses LLVM (22.1.5 in the toolchain line) and its hello-world startup is 0.113 s.
caveats: First-party benchmark in the author's own harness repo (borisbat/dasProfile, which shows no licence of its own). The kernels are separate per-language rewrites, and daslang is typed while Lua and JS are dynamic, so ratios mix language semantics with VM speed; some gaps (mandelbrot 32x, particles 41x vs Lua) look larger than interpreter design alone would give. DAS interpreter loses to LuaJIT -joff on tree and fibonacci recursive, and fibonacci recursive vs Lua is a 1.01x tie on Linux. Independent corroboration with weaker methodology: sashi0034/script-language-benchmark (Windows, Visual Studio 2022 Release, hardware not stated, README says it was written with Codex and not reviewed) shows Daslang beating Lua 5.5.0 and AngelScript on 13 of 16 workloads (fibonacci recursive 266 ms vs Lua 600 ms vs AngelScript 795 ms) but losing sort (237 ms vs Lua 6 ms) and string2float.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'AngelScript Squirrel ChaiScript Lua benchmark comparison embedded scripting performance fib github' surfaced sashi0034/script-language-benchmark; WebSearch 'daScript Daslang benchmark vs Lua LuaJIT performance' surfaced borisbat/dasProfile

name: nanobind
metric: compile-time; binary size (memory); call latency (runtime overhead)
workload: Large binding microbenchmark of 720 trivial functions (function-heavy) and the same computation packaged in structs (class-heavy): compile time, binary size and per-call overhead, in debug and size-optimised builds.
claimed_speedup: Up to ~4x faster compile (2.7-4.4x vs pybind11, 1.6-4.4x vs Cython), ~5x smaller binaries (3-5x vs pybind11, ~11x vs Boost.Python, 3-12x vs Cython), ~10x lower runtime overhead vs pybind11 (~3x for simple functions, ~10x when classes are passed around), 1.6-2.1x faster calls than cppyy; similar runtime to Cython.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 15.0.7, same flags for all libraries (listed in the plotting notebook docs/microbenchmark.ipynb, which I did not open), debug and -Os builds; Python 3.10.6, cppyy 1.12.13, Cython 0.29.28, nanobind 1.2.0
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X workstation, Ubuntu 22.04.2 LTS, CPU boost disabled and clocks pinned, median of five runs
stars_or_usage: 3.7k stars; adopted by JAX, XLA/MLIR, IREE, Apple MLX and FEniCS per the README testimonials
tradeoffs: Simplified feature set compared with pybind11 (overload resolution, C++ multiple inheritance and holder types were simplified or removed). Requires C++17 and a recent CPython; bindings are generated at compile time and ship as ordinary wheels.
caveats: The numbers come from nanobind 1.2.0 and Python 3.10 on one workstation; the author's own docs and a microbenchmark of trivial functions, so they measure binding overhead rather than application speed. The exact ratios live in SVG plots; the prose ratios above are quoted from the page. The baseline is not one of the category's listed incumbents (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS) and nanobind extends CPython from C++ rather than embedding a script engine, so a category move (for example to FFI or bindings) is plausible.
found_via: GitHub: binding-library angle (sol2 and LuaBridge3 are already catalogued as embedded scripting); opened wjakob/nanobind docs/benchmark.rst directly

name: SpiderMonkey (Mozilla)
baseline: QuickJS 2026-06-04 (also Duktape 2.99.99 on Ubuntu and macOS, 2.7.0 on Windows)
workload: V8 v7 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) combined score for SpiderMonkey shell 147.0 vs other engines, run by a daily GitHub Actions workflow on three operating systems.
claimed_speedup: Score on Ubuntu 19137 vs QuickJS 1217 and Duktape 489; macOS arm64 25455 vs QuickJS 1761 and Duktape 905; Windows 19049 vs QuickJS 1067 and Duktape 371 (about 15.7x, 14.5x and 17.9x vs QuickJS, derived from page data). Results dated 2026-10-05.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, macos-latest (arm64) and windows-latest runners; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 13.4k stars (mozilla-firefox/firefox); embedded via the SpiderMonkey C++ API (mozjs, spidermonkey-embedding-examples)
tradeoffs: Full JIT engine: shell binary 40.8M on Ubuntu and 134.9M on macOS vs QuickJS 1M and Duktape 370K, so score per MB is far lower (468/MB vs QuickJS 1190/MB). Building SpiderMonkey standalone is heavy; the repository is the whole Firefox tree with SpiderMonkey under js/src.
caveats: Independent but small third-party suite (59 stars) that runs prebuilt shells from its own spidermonkey-build repo, so compiler, flags and CPU are unknown. JIT engine vs interpreters, so the comparison says little about footprint-constrained use. I did not find a first-party SpiderMonkey claim against QuickJS. MPL-2.0 confirmed from the js/src/jsapi.h header; the repository LICENSE file only points to toolkit/content/license.html.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'embeddable JavaScript engine faster than QuickJS Duktape benchmark github C++ interpreter' surfaced ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark; harvested its winners

name: Ant (Ant Silver JavaScript engine)
baseline: QuickJS 2026-06-04 (also Duktape 2.99.99 / 2.7.0; its own README compares cold start against Node, Bun and Deno)
workload: V8 v7 benchmark suite combined score in the ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark daily CI; the project's own README separately times a Hono import cold start with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: Score on Ubuntu 2186 vs QuickJS 1217 and Duktape 489; macOS arm64 3589 vs 1761 and 905; Windows 2001 vs 1067 and 371 (about 1.8x, 2.0x and 1.9x vs QuickJS, derived from page data). README cold start: 3.9 ms vs Bun 8.8 ms, Deno 18.6 ms, Node 29.4 ms (Apple M5 Pro, hyperfine).
hardware: Shootout: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, macos-latest (arm64), windows-latest, CPU not stated. README cold-start test: Apple M5 Pro, 64 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Own engine (Ant Silver) with a JIT built on a MIR fork, packaged as a Node-style runtime of about 9-12 MB; test262 pass rate about 66% (35590 of 53578 at revision 2026-09-13). Binary is 11.7M on Ubuntu vs QuickJS 1M.
caveats: Ant is a runtime executable; I did not find a documented C or C++ embedding API, so use as an embedded scripting library is unverified. The shootout is a small third-party suite with prebuilt binaries, unknown flags and unknown CPU; the engine has a JIT while QuickJS and Duktape are interpreters. The README's own benchmark compares against Node, Bun and Deno, not the listed baselines.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/scripting-language and WebSearch 'embeddable JavaScript engine faster than QuickJS Duktape' led to ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark; harvested its winners over QuickJS

name: Quanta
baseline: Duktape 2.99.99 on Ubuntu and macOS, 2.7.0 on Windows (it is slower than QuickJS)
workload: V8 v7 benchmark suite combined score in the ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark daily CI, which the Quanta README links as its performance evidence.
claimed_speedup: Score on Ubuntu 1068 vs Duktape 489; macOS arm64 1118 vs 905; Windows 941 vs 371 (about 2.2x, 1.2x and 2.5x, derived from page data). Versus QuickJS it is slower: 1068 vs 1217, 1118 vs 1761, 941 vs 1067. Results dated 2026-10-05.
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, macos-latest (arm64), windows-latest runners; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Experimental ECMAScript engine with an embedding API (recent commits add host-hook module loading and DefineGlobalFunction). Binary 5.6M on Ubuntu vs Duktape 370K and QuickJS 1M.
caveats: Experimental, very low stars, and slower than QuickJS on all three platforms, so it is worth listing only against Duktape. Evidence is the same small third-party suite with prebuilt binaries and unknown flags and CPU. The README claims 'memory efficiency and execution speed' but gives no numbers of its own. Recent commit listings show a collaborator account named claude.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=c++ listed solarbrowser/quanta; its README links the js-engine-benchmark page

name: Escargot (Samsung)
baseline: QuickJS 2026-06-04 (also V8 d8 and V8 --jitless in the same report)
workload: Monthly CI engine comparison on ARM64: SunSpider (26 scripts, mean of 5 fresh processes), Octane (one score run), Web Tooling Benchmark (18 workloads) for speed, and fixed-work RSS (median of three fresh processes) for memory.
claimed_speedup: Report measured 2026-10-04: SunSpider 823.2 ms vs QuickJS 981.6 ms, Octane 2,198 vs 1,689, Web Tooling 1.07 vs 0.89 runs/s (about 1.19x, 1.30x and 1.20x, derived from page data). Average RSS: Octane 85.7 vs 161.4 MiB, Web Tooling 171.6 vs 375.9 MiB; SunSpider is the other way, 14.2 vs 5.3 MiB.
compiler_and_flags: Escargot built as monthly-engine-release-arm64 (flags not stated); QuickJS 2026-06-04 from Bellard's tarball run as qjs --std with an 8 MiB stack; the same glibc 2.39 runtime for all engines; suite revisions are pinned in the JSON
hardware: aarch64 Linux host (platform string Linux-6.8.0-1063-aws-aarch64), workloads pinned to CPU 0 with a separate monitor CPU; CPU model not named in the data
stars_or_usage: 364 stars; Samsung says it ships in its products, Tizen is a listed target
tradeoffs: Bytecode interpreter with no JIT or executable memory needed, ES2026 plus Intl and Temporal through ICU (extra dependency or size), C++ API in src/api/EscargotPublic.h, also a Node-API hosting layer and RTOS ports. LGPL-2.1 with some Apache-2.0, BSD, MIT and MPL components.
caveats: First-party CI report whose build flags and CPU model are not stated, so it falls short of tier A; the raw JSON, commands and logs are published, which makes it checkable. Speed gain is modest (about 1.2-1.3x) and memory is worse than QuickJS on small scripts (SunSpider). The dashboard page on samsung.github.io was blocked, so I read the same data from the gh-pages branch through raw.githubusercontent.com.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/javascript-engine?l=c++ listed Samsung/escargot; README links to the monthly comparison dashboard

name: Ravi
baseline: Lua 5.3 (the dialect it extends; LuaJIT is named as a different-goal alternative)
workload: No benchmark numbers on the pages I opened; the README says optional static typing lets the JIT (MIR, LLVM backends) generate faster code, and a matmul1_ravi.lua benchmark program is in ravi-tests.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: 'static typing for improved performance when JIT compilation is enabled'. The same README says Ravi prioritises maintenance, language safety and Lua 5.3 compatibility over maximum performance.
tradeoffs: Dialect of Lua with optional type annotations (not a drop-in for LuaJIT-style Lua 5.1 code); JIT backend is MIR, with AOT compilation to shared libraries; Lua 5.4 generational GC backported. Compatible with Lua 5.3 programs.
caveats: Tier D entry kept because the project is notable (over 1k stars) and explicitly claims a JIT speedup from typing; no benchmark page was found in the README or readthedocs folder (the old ravi-benchmarks page returns 404). Verifiers should look in ravi-tests and the issue tracker for numbers before keeping it at D.
